opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it was that I tried to work on problems that felt important but were still a bit underdefined. When I started my PhD, around 2019 and 2020, language models were getting powerful, but most people were still treating them as tools for specific NLP tasks: classification, QA, translation. I was more interested in a different question: what does it look like for a language model to actually *act* in the world, to make decisions, interact with an environment, and reason over many steps?

So a lot of my work, like text-based games, WebShop, ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, and later SWE-bench, came from that one thread. In hindsight, having a consistent question, rather than chasing whatever benchmark was hot, helped a lot. Each project built on the last one, and I had an intuition for where things were going.

The second thing is that I cared a lot about simplicity. ReAct, for example, is a very simple idea: let the model interleave reasoning and acting. A simple idea that is general is often more valuable than a complicated method that gets a few more points on one dataset. Simple ideas get adopted, people build on them, and they survive when models get better. Complicated tricks usually get washed away by the next generation of models.

The third thing is that I spent a lot of time thinking about evaluation and environments, not just methods. People often underrate this. If you define a good task, like a realistic web environment or real GitHub issues, you are shaping what the whole field optimizes for. I think in the next phase of AI that matters even more, because the methods are becoming quite general, and the real question becomes: what problems should we solve, and how do we know we've solved them?

And finally, I was lucky to be at Princeton with advisors like Karthik Narasimhan, who gave me a lot of freedom, and with collaborators who were willing to bet on these somewhat weird directions early. Being early on the right question matters more than being smart on the wrong one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I didn't fully know what I was doing for the first couple of years, and the thing that saved me was being a bit stubborn about one question.

When I started at Princeton, the field was dominated by reinforcement learning on games, and I was interested in language because it felt like the natural interface for agents. That was not a popular combination at the time. Language people thought agents were a toy, and RL people thought text environments were a distraction. So I spent a lot of my early PhD building things like text games and interactive environments, which didn't produce big results right away. But it forced me to think carefully about what an agent actually is: something that observes, reasons, and acts in a loop. That framing stayed with me.

The second thing was timing and taste. When large language models started getting really capable, I didn't try to compete on scale, because obviously a PhD student can't. Instead I asked, what's the simplest thing you could do with this model that makes it an agent? ReAct came out of that. It's almost embarrassingly simple, just interleaving thinking and acting in the prompt. But it worked, and it gave people a mental model. Same with Tree of Thoughts, same with SWE-bench. In each case the idea was to find the minimal thing that changes how people see the problem, rather than the most complicated thing.

And the third thing is that I cared a lot about evaluation, maybe more than about methods. A good benchmark defines a problem so clearly that the whole community can work on it. WebShop and SWE-bench were as much about saying, this is what we should be measuring, as they were about any particular technique. Looking back, I think choosing the right problems to work on mattered far more than being clever about how to solve them.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think it was a combination of following my curiosity and being willing to change my mind. In AI research, you need a direction, but you also need to notice when an experiment is telling you that your original question wasn’t quite the right one.

One thing I found useful was moving between concrete experiments and broader questions. You build something, see where it fails, and then ask: Is this just an implementation problem, or does it reveal something missing in how we’re thinking about intelligence? That back-and-forth can be more productive than trying to develop a complete theory before you start.

And the people around you matter a lot. Conversations with advisors and collaborators help turn a vague intuition into a question you can actually test. I wouldn’t attribute a fruitful PhD to a single approach—it’s curiosity, feedback, and having the space to pursue something before it’s obvious that it will work.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I think it helped that I was willing to follow a question even when I didn’t know what the final research project would look like. A PhD gives you some room to do that—to explore, get stuck, and gradually figure out which questions are worth pursuing.

For me, a recurring question was how language models could do more than produce an answer: how they could reason, interact with an environment, and learn from feedback. That gave my work a direction, while leaving room to change the specific approach as the models improved.

I also think there’s value in moving between a big-picture question and a very concrete experiment. The big question helps you choose what matters, but implementing something forces you to confront what actually works. And conversations with collaborators are essential—you might have an intuition, but explaining it to someone else often reveals what’s missing.
